title: Where Quantum Fourier Sampling Stops Short: A Three-Gate Audit Protocol for Delay-PUF Security Models
authors: Owen Friedewald, Ali Shiri Sichani, Chi-Ren Shyu
abstract: Quantum Fourier sampling may help audit the spectral learnability of delay-based physical unclonable functions (PUFs). We ask whether that promise survives access matching, a strong classical comparator, and oracle synthesis. Three gates structure the evaluation. Structure: low degree is not small support at reachable challenge lengths; for 4-XOR at $n=14$, degree $\le d_f(0.1)$ admits $91\%$ of all $2^n$ characters and the median $90\%$-mass set spans a third of the spectrum. Algorithmics: constructing the phase oracle logically implies classical membership access, making Kushilevitz--Mansour the correct baseline; across 45 tasks it exhausts each finite domain, and no 4-XOR ideal-sampling case reaches $90\%$ mass within $2^n$ calls. A quantum-kernel diagnostic appears more favorable, with geometric difference rising to $2.151$ at $N=512$ challenges, but it correlates $0.991$ with $1/\sqrt{λ_{\min}(K_C)}$ for the classical Gram matrix $K_C$, and the 4-XOR label-complexity ratio does not exceed a balance-preserving permutation null ($p=0.930$). Trace-normalized geometric difference can therefore grow through classical ill-conditioning alone, without task-label alignment. Implementation: a simulator-validated fixed-point phase oracle based on the quantum Fourier transform admits an $18.9\%$ routed-depth reduction, yet the least certified precisions have estimated durations of $1.18$--$1.55\times$ the median dephasing time $T_2$ of the mapped qubits on a static backend snapshot, without hardware execution. We find no end-to-end advantage in the evaluated regime, although ideal sampling does use fewer coherent calls on the thresholded task. The contribution is the Three-Gate Quantum Audit Protocol: a reproducible procedure separating an ideal query advantage from a realizable security benefit. This is not a claim about deployed silicon and not an impossibility result.
summary: This paper develops a 'Three-Gate Quantum Audit Protocol' to test if Quantum Fourier Sampling offers a genuine security advantage when auditing delay-based PUFs. By analyzing structural, algorithmic, and implementation constraints, the authors conclude that no end-to-end quantum advantage was found in their simulated, evaluated regime. This work establishes a rigorous diagnostic tool for assessing the feasibility of quantum machine learning in physical security applications.
main_problem: The paper audits the theoretical promise of using Quantum Fourier Sampling (QFS) to assess the spectral learnability of delay-based Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs). It determines the practical limits where this quantum advantage breaks down against strong classical comparators and hardware constraints.
main_result: The Three-Gate Quantum Audit Protocol finds no end-to-end advantage for QFS in the evaluated regime, suggesting that ideal quantum query advantages do not translate into realizable security benefits for these PUF models.
method: The authors employ a structured 'Three-Gate' protocol (Structural, Algorithmic, Implementation) comparing QFS against classical membership access (Kushilevitz–Mansour) and analyzing resource costs using simulated quantum circuits (QFT).
model_or_system: The study models delay-based PUFs (Additive-delay APUF and XOR-APUF) and analyzes their spectral properties using quantum Fourier transforms and associated quantum kernels.
key_observables: Asymmetric geometric difference between classical and quantum Gram matrices ($g(\mathbf{K}_C\|\mathbf{K}_Q)$), spectral mass recovery percentage, and estimated circuit depth/duration relative to the qubit coherence time ($T_2$).
important_parameters: Challenge length ($n$), concentration threshold ($\epsilon$), and the degree of the polynomial structure ($d$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to a design-time model audit using a simulated, fixed-point phase oracle, not a claim about deployed silicon.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate resource tradeoffs (e.g., depth vs. precision) and show quantitative comparisons of performance metrics (mass/recall) between classical and quantum sampling methods across different PUF types.
paper_structure: The paper is structured around the Three-Gate Audit Protocol: first, establishing structural bounds; second, comparing QFS against classical algorithms using kernel diagnostics; and third, evaluating resource feasibility using simulated quantum circuits.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, multi-faceted framework for determining the boundary between theoretical quantum advantage and practical, implementable security guarantees in quantum-enhanced cryptography.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Finite-n concentration sweep with 30 deterministic seeded PUF instances per cell. Lines are medians and shaded bands are interquartile ranges across instances. Left: the fraction of all 2n characters admitted by degree ≤df(0.1). Right: the fraction needed to accumulate 90% Fourier mass. For higher XOR counts, both denominators remain large rather than shrinking toward a sparse audit target.

Figure 2: Precision and resource tradeoffs over three PUF instances and three transpiler seeds per point; accuracy is worst-instance and routed cost is the median. “Frozen gate” denotes a criterion fixed before the sweep. Dashed lines show these thresholds. Signal-preserving precision arrives only after median circuit duration reaches or exceeds mapped median T2. Transpilation only; no backend execution.
